extracted.intended_audience: Users and developers of the Rocq Prover / Coq who write proofs, libraries or plugins
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and conventions for using Rocq/Coq standard libraries, the prelude, notations, datatypes, recursion and tactics when developing proofs, libraries or projects in Rocq.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core library / preloaded files
rubrics_metrics.description: The core library contains definitions and theorems for the most commonly used elementary logical notions and data types, primitive objects, and support for tactics/commands (e.g., setoid_rewrite, Program, ssreflect, Ltac2). Rocq automatically loads many of these files when it starts; this set of preloaded files is called the prelude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The content of the corelib and the prelude can be browsed online (corelib and Corelib.Init.Prelude). Rely on corelib for basic primitives and commonly used constructions; expect many corelib files to be available without explicit loading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit loading of standard library files
rubrics_metrics.description: Other libraries like the standard library are general-purpose libraries (sets, lists, arithmetic, etc.) that are not automatically loaded and must be loaded explicitly by the user.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To use standard library files, load them with an explicit command such as 'From Stdlib Require ...' (see the Compiled files section).

rubrics_metrics.name: Notations: purpose and precedence/associativity rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The Notations module defines parsing and pretty-printing of many symbols (infixes, prefixes) but does not assign semantic meaning; its purpose is to fix precedence and associativity of very common notations in the initial state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the predefined precedence and associativity table when writing code to avoid ambiguity. The documentation lists the main notations and their precedence/associativity (examples: '->' precedence 99 right; '<->' 95 no; '\/' 85 right; '/\' 80 right; '~' 75 right; '=' 70 no; '+' 50 left; '*' 40 left; '^' 30 right; '-' and '/' at 35 right).

rubrics_metrics.name: Zero notation: O vs 0
rubrics_metrics.description: In Coq's standard definitions zero is the letter 'O' (capital O), not the numeral '0'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing natural-number values or pattern-matching on nats, use O for zero. Decimal notation is also provided (see nat_scope) so decimal numerals may be used as sugar, but the canonical constructor is O.

rubrics_metrics.name: nat_scope and decimal notation for numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: The Peano module provides a scope nat_scope gathering standard notations for common operations (+, *, etc.) and a decimal notation for numbers; nat_scope is opened by default.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may write decimal numerals (e.g., 3) as sugar for S (S (S O)); decimal notation also works on the left-hand side of match expressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recursive/guarded Fixpoint definitions and termination discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Recursive functions (Fixpoint) must be structurally/guardedly defined so that termination is evident to the system; examples show recursion guarded on the first argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure recursive definitions are accepted by the guard checker (struct annotation). For more complex termination, use well-founded recursion tools (Acc/well_founded) described in Wf.v and Fix/Fix_F constructs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-founded recursion and Fix via Acc
rubrics_metrics.description: The Wf module provides Acc, well_founded and machinery to define functions by fixpoints justified by well-founded relations, together with well-founded induction principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To define functions that are not structurally recursive, prove a relation well_founded and use the provided Fix/Fix_F scheme (Acc_intro, Fix_F_eq, Fix_eq). Ensure any extensionality hypotheses required for equality of fixpoints are satisfied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependent sums: sig (Prop) vs sigT (Type)
rubrics_metrics.description: sig (notation { x : A | P x }) is a weak dependent sum producing a Type when P : A -> Prop; the justification (proof) is hidden and not extractable. sigT (existT) is the strong dependent sum for P : A -> Type, residing in Type and exposing both witness and evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose sig when the second component is a Prop and you want the proof to remain hidden (abstract); use sigT when the second component is a Type and you need to access both parts. Use projT1/projT2 to extract witness and (when available) the second component from sigT values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive sums for decidability: sumbool and sumor
rubrics_metrics.description: sumbool implements a constructive sum {A} + {B} of two propositions as a Set (left/right with evidence), useful to represent decidability; sumor mixes a Type/Set component with a Prop (A +{B}).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sumbool as an indexed boolean-like datatype when you need an explicit decidability result (left/right constructors). Use sumor when combining a data component (Set) with a proposition (Prop).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality: inductive eq and associated lemmas
rubrics_metrics.description: Equality is defined as an inductive relation eq with constructor eq_refl; standard lemmas and eliminators (eq_rect, eq_ind, eq_sym, eq_trans, f_equal, f_equal2..f_equal5) are provided in the basic library.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the provided equality lemmas and registers (Hint Immediate eq_sym not_eq_sym : core) and the f_equal family when reasoning about equalities under functions of several arguments. Use the eq_ind/_rect variants for elimination/transport tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specif constructs and usage (exist, existT, projections)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specif.v supplies constructs such as { x : A | P x } (sig), exist, existT and projection utilities (projT1, projT2); exist builds a witness + justification; from exist you can extract the witness but not the justification for sig.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When pattern-matching on exist/existT values use match/return idioms as shown in examples; use the provided projection functions to extract components when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sumbool-based choice and choice lemmas
rubrics_metrics.description: The basic library provides variants of the axiom of choice and lemmas (Choice, Choice2, bool_choice) making use of constructive dependent sums and sumbool to build choice functions under constructive hypotheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing constructive choice proofs, use the provided lemmas to convert local existence/decidability hypotheses into functions or boolean-valued choices as illustrated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tactics provided in initial state and tactic-language support
rubrics_metrics.description: A few tactics are provided at user level in the initial state (Tactics module of Corelib); the documentation also documents ssreflect, Ltac2 and many tactic support facilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on the preloaded tactic support for common proof patterns; consult the Tactics/ssreflect/Ltac2 sections for usage, compatibility issues and migration guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opam repository and user-contributed packages
rubrics_metrics.description: Many user contributions are packaged and available in the Rocq Opam repository with metadata (author, institution, description) and can be downloaded or installed with opam.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Browse the packages page for existing libraries, installation instructions and information on how to submit new packages to the repository.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notation conflicts and overriding
rubrics_metrics.description: Notations can conflict or be overridden; the system may issue warnings when a notation (e.g., '_ <= _' in nat_scope) is already used and gets overridden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful when declaring new notations or importing modules that introduce notations; check for warnings and prefer reserving/qualifying notations to avoid accidental overrides.
